case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under the Federal Arbitration Act, a federal court may compel arbitration when the party seeking arbitration did not timely raise (and thus forfeited) its arbitration-right argument in the lower courts, or whether the court of appeals properly refused to consider that newly presented legal theory on appeal under ordinary forfeiture principles.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16 (especially §§ 2–4 governing enforceability of arbitration agreements and motions to compel), along with federal appellate forfeiture/waiver doctrines (judge-made procedural rules rather than a single statute).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Flowers Foods and the other petitioners contend that the FAA’s pro-arbitration policy and its command to enforce arbitration agreements require courts to order arbitration once an agreement covering the dispute is shown, and that the Tenth Circuit should have reached and accepted their arbitration argument even if it was not properly preserved below; they further argue that refusing to consider the arbitration point because of forfeiture improperly elevates procedural default over the FAA’s substantive enforcement mandate and creates uncertainty for businesses that rely on arbitration clauses.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Brock argues that the FAA does not displace ordinary principles of issue preservation and forfeiture on appeal; because petitioners failed to timely raise the relevant arbitration theory in the district court (and/or otherwise failed to properly present it), the court of appeals correctly treated it as forfeited and declined to consider it, consistent with settled appellate practice that only rarely excuses forfeiture for purely legal issues whose correct resolution is beyond reasonable doubt.
key_precedents: United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007)
Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir. 2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest contention is that the FAA’s mandatory “shall” language in §§ 3–4, coupled with § 16(a)’s interlocutory appeal, requires courts of appeals to correct any erroneous denial of arbitration even on a theory raised for the first time on appeal. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, § 6 directs that FAA motions proceed “in the manner provided by law,” which incorporates the ordinary party-presentation and forfeiture regime rather than creating an arbitration-specific exemption. Reading §§ 2–4 against that settled procedural backdrop, § 16(a) authorizes appellate review; it does not impose an obligation to entertain new arguments neither pressed nor passed upon below, and Morgan cautions against crafting arbitration-favoring procedural carveouts. The Tenth Circuit therefore acted within traditional appellate discretion in applying forfeiture to an unpreserved theory.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that §§3–4 use mandatory language (“shall”) and thus an appellate court must correct an erroneous denial of arbitration even on a newly minted theory. But that argument reads the operative commands in isolation from the settled procedural backdrop Congress left in place: as Justice Kagan persuasively notes, §6 instructs courts to proceed “in the manner provided by law,” which incorporates ordinary party-presentation and forfeiture rules rather than displacing them. Nothing in the FAA’s text creates an arbitration-specific exception to those background principles, and adopting one would give arbitration agreements more favorable procedural treatment than other contracts—contrary to the Act’s equal-footing rule and our reasoning in Morgan, as the Chief Justice emphasizes. The Tenth Circuit therefore acted within traditional appellate discretion in declining to consider an argument neither pressed nor passed upon below.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that §§ 3–4 use mandatory language—courts “shall” stay litigation and compel arbitration—so an appellate court ought to order arbitration whenever the statutory predicates are met, even if the decisive theory was not raised below. But, as Justice Kagan explains, § 6 instructs that FAA motions proceed “in the manner provided by law,” which incorporates ordinary party-presentation and forfeiture principles rather than displacing them; nothing in §§ 2–4 or § 16 creates an arbitration-specific exemption from those background rules. Treating arbitration as uniquely nonforfeitable would, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh note, make arbitration agreements more enforceable than other contracts—precisely the arbitration-favoring procedural tilt Morgan rejects—and would invite strategic sandbagging. On these facts, the Tenth Circuit acted within settled appellate discretion in declining to entertain a newly minted theory first raised on appeal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that the FAA’s mandatory “shall” language and §16’s interlocutory appeal mechanism reflect a policy of prompt arbitration enforcement, so appellate courts should reach any legal theory that would compel arbitration. But as Justice Kagan explains, §6’s instruction to proceed “in the manner provided by law” incorporates ordinary motion practice—including issue-preservation—rather than creating an arbitration-specific exception, and the Chief Justice correctly notes that inventing such an exemption would privilege arbitration agreements over other contracts in tension with Morgan’s equal-treatment principle. The real-world consequences also matter: excusing forfeiture here invites strategic sandbagging and imposes disproportionate costs and delay on less-resourced litigants who must relitigate on shifting grounds. Consistent with Justice Gorsuch’s “pressed or passed upon” point, the Tenth Circuit acted within settled discretion in declining to consider an argument neither raised nor developed below.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that § 16(a)’s interlocutory-appeal authorization (paired with the “shall” language in §§ 3–4) reflects Congress’s desire for prompt correction of erroneous denials of arbitration, so courts of appeals should reach any meritorious ground to compel even if raised late. But, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, nothing in § 16 (or elsewhere in the FAA) speaks to displacing ordinary preservation rules, and § 6’s command to proceed on FAA motions “in the manner provided by law” instead incorporates the normal federal framework of party presentation and forfeiture. Justice Kavanaugh’s “background rules” point is decisive here: Congress legislated against a settled procedural backdrop in which new theories generally cannot be debuted on appeal, and Morgan cautions against inventing arbitration-specific procedural carveouts like a nonforfeiture rule. The Tenth Circuit thus acted within traditional appellate discretion in declining to entertain a theory neither pressed nor passed upon below.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest contention is that the FAA’s mandatory “shall” language and § 16(a)’s interlocutory-appeal mechanism require appellate courts to reach any arbitration-enforcement theory, preserved or not, to avoid wrongful litigation. But as Justice Kagan persuasively notes, § 6 instructs courts to proceed “in the manner provided by law,” which incorporates ordinary motion practice—including forfeiture principles—rather than displacing them. On our settled “pressed or passed upon” rule, this theory was neither pressed in the district court nor passed upon there, and—consistent with the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s points—nothing in the FAA warrants inventing an arbitration-specific exemption that would make arbitration agreements more enforceable than other contracts, contrary to Morgan’s equal-footing principle. Nor does this case present the kind of structural or third-party-rights concern that might justify overlooking forfeiture under the limited exceptions recognized in cases like Freytag.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that the FAA’s mandatory “shall” language and §16(a)’s interlocutory appeal reflect a pro-enforcement design that should lead courts of appeals to reach any meritorious arbitration theory, preserved or not. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the statute is silent on preservation and §6 instructs courts to proceed “in the manner provided by law,” which incorporates settled party-presentation and forfeiture principles rather than displacing them. Reading the FAA against that background procedural regime, §16(a) creates an appeal right, not an arbitration-specific exemption from ordinary appellate practice; and, as Morgan reinforces, we should not invent arbitration-favoring procedural carveouts that would make arbitration agreements more enforceable than other contracts. Functionally, allowing first-time-on-appeal pivots would invite sandbagging and frustrate orderly case management, so the Tenth Circuit acted within traditional discretion in declining to reach an unpreserved theory.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is the mandatory “shall” language in §§ 3–4, coupled with § 16(a), which they say requires appellate correction even when the dispositive theory was not preserved. But as Justice Kagan stresses, § 6 instructs courts to proceed “in the manner provided by law,” which naturally incorporates the ordinary party-presentation and forfeiture rules rather than silently creating an arbitration-specific exception. Reading the FAA against that procedural backdrop, nothing in the statute converts an interlocutory appeal into a vehicle for new theories, and (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh note) doing so would give arbitration agreements a procedural advantage other contracts do not enjoy—tension with Morgan’s equal-footing principle. On these facts, the Tenth Circuit acted within settled appellate discretion in declining to reach an unpreserved § 1 argument.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest claim—that FAA § 1’s carveout is so fundamental that it must be addressed even if raised late—still fails because nothing in the FAA’s text or structure displaces ordinary issue-preservation principles. As Justice Kagan explains, § 6’s command to proceed “in the manner provided by law” incorporates the usual forfeiture framework rather than authorizing an arbitration-specific exemption, and Morgan cautions against judicially crafting arbitration-favoring procedural rules. The mandatory “shall” language in §§ 3–4, highlighted by Justice Thomas, operates once properly invoked; it does not transform appellate review into an obligation to entertain brand-new theories neither pressed nor passed upon below. On this record, enforcing forfeiture accords with settled party-presentation norms and treats arbitration agreements on equal footing with other contracts.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FAA’s operative text requires courts to enforce arbitration agreements “save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity,” but it does not purport to displace ordinary appellate issue-preservation rules or compel courts of appeals to entertain legal theories first raised on appeal. Applying our procedural first principles, the court of appeals properly treated petitioners’ newly presented arbitration-right theory as forfeited and declined to reach it, because nothing in §§ 2–4 confers a special exemption from forfeiture or converts arbitration into a nonforfeitable entitlement. Consistent with Steel Co.’s insistence on following the “proper path” dictated by governing rules, we should not rewrite background appellate practice in the name of a generalized pro-arbitration policy—especially after Morgan v. Sundance made clear the FAA makes arbitration agreements enforceable like other contracts, not more so. On these facts, petitioners’ failure to timely press the controlling arbitration argument in the district court means the court of appeals acted within settled discretion in refusing to consider it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAA’s operative text requires courts to enforce arbitration agreements on the same “equal footing” as other contracts, not to give arbitration a special procedural preference that displaces ordinary federal rules of issue preservation. Nothing in §§2–4 commands a court of appeals to entertain a newly minted arbitration theory first raised on appeal, and longstanding forfeiture doctrine is a background procedural principle that the FAA does not purport to abrogate. Petitioners’ request would effectively create an arbitration-specific exception to forfeiture—exactly the kind of judge-made expansion inconsistent with the FAA’s equal-treatment rule and with limited judicial role principles. Because petitioners failed to timely present the pertinent arbitration-right argument below, the Tenth Circuit acted within settled appellate practice in declining to consider it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The question is not jurisdictional: the FAA’s §§ 3–4 supply enforcement mechanisms when a party timely invokes arbitration, but they do not impose on appellate courts an independent obligation to entertain newly minted arbitration theories sua sponte. Under ordinary party-presentation and forfeiture principles, a court of appeals may (and generally should) decline to consider an argument first raised on appeal, and nothing in the FAA makes arbitration rights uniquely immune from forfeiture; indeed, the FAA makes arbitration agreements enforceable like other contracts, not “more so.” Compelling arbitration here would effectively allow a litigant to expand its contractual arbitration right through procedural default rules, contrary to the consent-based nature of arbitration and settled appellate practice. The Tenth Circuit therefore acted properly in refusing to reach petitioners’ forfeited arbitration-right theory.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FAA’s command to enforce arbitration agreements does not grant a party a procedural free pass to sandbag an opponent by withholding its arbitration theory in the district court and unveiling it only on appeal. Ordinary forfeiture principles promote fairness, accurate fact development, and access to justice—especially for individuals who may lack resources to relitigate issues after an appellate pivot—and nothing in the FAA’s text requires courts of appeals to excuse a litigant’s failure to timely raise an argument. Here, petitioners’ newly presented arbitration-right theory was not preserved below, and the court of appeals acted within settled discretion in refusing to consider it, rather than using “pro-arbitration policy” to override basic procedural regularity. Enforcing forfeiture in these circumstances safeguards real-world reliance on orderly litigation and prevents arbitration from becoming a tool of strategic delay or surprise against a vulnerable litigant.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Nothing in the FAA’s text or structure displaces the ordinary rule that arguments not timely raised in the district court are forfeited on appeal. Section 6 directs courts to handle arbitration-related motions “in the manner provided by law” for motions generally, which points to applying the usual preservation/forfeiture doctrines rather than inventing an arbitration-specific exception requiring appellate courts to reach new theories. Petitioners’ reliance on a generalized pro-arbitration policy asks for exactly the kind of arbitration-preferring procedural carveout we rejected in Morgan: the FAA makes arbitration agreements enforceable like other contracts, not more so. Because petitioners first advanced the decisive arbitration theory only on appeal, the court of appeals acted within ordinary federal practice in declining to consider it and therefore in refusing to compel arbitration on that forfeited ground.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners concede they did not present in the district court their dispositive FAA § 1 “contract of employment” theory (that the Distributor Agreement is not a contract of employment), so the argument was at least forfeited, and nothing in the record suggests an intentional relinquishment issue that would alter the analysis. Under this Court’s ordinary practice, an appellate court generally relies on forfeiture when an issue was “not pressed or passed upon” below; here, the theory was neither pressed by petitioners nor passed upon by the district court, leaving the Tenth Circuit on firm ground to decline review. The FAA’s command to enforce arbitration agreements does not erase settled preservation rules governing what arguments a party must timely present to obtain that relief, especially where (as the Tenth Circuit found) the newly minted theory raises a question of first impression and is not “beyond reasonable doubt.” Nor does this case present the sort of structural concern or third-party rights problem that might justify overlooking forfeiture under the limited discretion recognized in cases like Freytag.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FAA’s text and structure require enforcement of arbitration agreements when properly invoked, but they are silent about displacing the settled “background” procedural rule that parties must timely present their legal theories in the district court and ordinarily may not raise a new theory for the first time on appeal. Reading the FAA against that clear procedural backdrop, the court of appeals permissibly applied ordinary forfeiture principles in declining to entertain petitioners’ newly presented arbitration theory—especially where the argument turned on a first-impression question in the circuit and thus was not “beyond reasonable doubt,” making this unlike the rare case where forfeiture is excused. Nothing in §§ 2–4 or § 16(a)’s interlocutory-appeal authorization suggests Congress intended to convert an appeal from the denial of arbitration into a vehicle for sandbagging new statutory theories that were not litigated below. Functionally, allowing such late-raised FAA theories would undermine orderly case management and appellate review by encouraging parallel tracks of litigation positions rather than resolving the arbitration issue as framed and developed in the district court.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Nothing in the FAA’s text—particularly §§ 2–4—purports to displace ordinary rules of issue preservation on appeal; those provisions speak to the enforceability of arbitration agreements and the mechanism for compelling arbitration when a party properly invokes that right, not to reopening forfeited theories. Reading the FAA to require appellate courts to entertain newly minted arbitration arguments would create a procedural mismatch with settled forfeiture doctrine and make arbitration agreements “more so” enforceable than other contracts, contrary to the FAA’s equal-treatment principle. On these facts, petitioners failed to timely present their dispositive arbitration theory in the lower courts, so the court of appeals acted within ordinary discretion in declining to consider it absent the narrow, exceptional circumstances that sometimes justify reaching forfeited purely legal issues. The FAA’s pro-arbitration policy cannot supply atextual authorization to override routine appellate practice.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying ordinary issue-preservation principles, the Tenth Circuit properly declined to entertain Flowers’s newly pressed theory that the Distributor Agreement is not a “contract of employment” under FAA § 1, because Flowers concededly failed to raise that argument in the district court and thus forfeited it on appeal. Nothing in the FAA’s text or structure in §§ 2–4 purports to displace standard appellate forfeiture rules or to require courts to reach unpreserved arbitration theories; the Act directs enforcement of arbitration agreements only through the ordinary procedural channels litigants must properly invoke. Consistent with Morgan, courts should not invent arbitration-specific procedural preferences that excuse forfeiture merely because the late-raised argument seeks arbitration. And under the Tenth Circuit’s own standards (Jarvis/Ave. Cap.), there was no obligation to overlook forfeiture absent a purely legal issue whose correct resolution is beyond reasonable doubt, which Flowers did not establish here.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the court of appeals properly affirmed (or could consider) a legal theory supporting liability that the respondent did not adequately preserve below, under appellate forfeiture/waiver principles and the governing federal labor/employment statute at issue in the underlying misclassification dispute.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal appellate preservation doctrine (forfeiture/waiver) as applied on appeal; the underlying federal labor/employment statute governing the employee/independent-contractor classification dispute (not specified in the provided excerpts).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Tenth Circuit improperly entertained and resolved a forfeited argument—i.e., a legal theory not timely raised/preserved—thereby expanding liability based on a new appellate theory and contravening the usual rule that unpreserved arguments are not considered on appeal except in narrow circumstances.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the issue the Tenth Circuit considered was a pure question of law whose correct resolution is clear/certain, fitting within the circuit’s discretionary exception for considering forfeited legal arguments; respondent’s amici further contend that the court’s approach aligns with proper statutory interpretation and remedial purposes in the employment context.
key_precedents: United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007)
Avenue Capital Management II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that we ordinarily do not take up factbound, circuit-specific applications of forfeiture doctrine, and that we are a court of review, not first view. But this is not merely discretionary line-drawing: the Tenth Circuit invoked a self-imposed, highly demanding “pure matter of law/answer is certain” exception to affirm liability on a concededly unpreserved theory in a misclassification setting where the “certainty” premise is difficult to maintain without trial-level development. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, the absence of adversarial testing and district-court consideration makes it hard to say the correct resolution is “beyond reasonable doubt,” and our usual remand-first principles counsel against appellate merits determinations on an unpassed-upon ground. A narrow holding enforcing the preservation constraint—and vacating/remanding for proper application of the circuit’s own stringent exception—respects institutional role-allocation without turning us into supervisors of routine forfeiture administration.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press the best point against my view: that the Tenth Circuit’s “pure question of law/answer is certain” exception is demanding and seems ill-suited to a misclassification setting, making this look like a structural departure rather than a mere case-specific call. But that argument still asks us to police, in the first instance, whether the Tenth Circuit misapplied its own Jarvis/Schaden preservation framework to this record—precisely the sort of factbound, discretionary administration of forfeiture rules that seldom warrants our intervention, especially where the petitioners’ merits objections do the real work. And accepting petitioners’ framing would pull us into deciding whether the alternative theory was indeed “certain” on an undeveloped record, contravening our role as a court of review rather than first view. Absent a clearly reviewable legal rule of decision announced by the Tenth Circuit (as opposed to an arguable misapplication), I would leave the court of appeals’ preservation determination undisturbed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that we ordinarily do not take up a court of appeals’ case-specific administration of its own forfeiture doctrine, and that doing so risks turning us into a court of first view. But this is not a marginal, discretionary call: the Tenth Circuit affirmed liability on a concededly unpreserved theory, and its own “pure question of law/answer is certain” exception is a demanding legal standard that cannot plausibly be satisfied in a misclassification setting without trial-level development. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, declaring the answer “certain” here effectively relaxes party-presentation and invites appellate courts to rescue forfeited merits theories—something preservation rules are designed to prevent. Because the forfeiture rule is nonjurisdictional, it is precisely the sort of claim-processing principle that should be enforced when timely invoked, not circumvented to expand liability on an untested ground.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that we typically do not police a court of appeals’ discretionary administration of forfeiture, especially where the complaint is case-specific line-drawing. But this record is not about marginal discretion: the respondent concedes nonpreservation, petitioners timely pressed forfeiture, and the district court did not “pass upon” the alternative liability theory—so affirmance rests on an issue neither raised nor developed below. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Tenth Circuit’s own “pure question of law/answer is certain” exception cannot coherently be satisfied in a misclassification setting without factfinding and adversarial testing, and treating it as satisfied risks turning a prudential forfeiture doctrine into appellate first-instance merits decisionmaking. The proper course, consistent with our court-of-review role and Article III limits, is to vacate or reverse and require adherence to preservation rules rather than endorse liability on a newly minted theory.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to caution that we usually do not second-guess a court of appeals’ administration of its own forfeiture doctrine. But this is not a close, record-bound call: respondent concedes non-preservation, and the Tenth Circuit’s own Jarvis/Schaden exception permits review only for a pure legal issue whose correct resolution is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt”—a threshold that, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, is ill-suited to a misclassification theory requiring application of law to an undeveloped factual record. Ordinary preservation principles exist to protect party presentation and the trial–appellate division of labor, and nothing in the governing statute supplies a carve-out allowing affirmance on a forfeited liability theory. The proper course is to enforce forfeiture (or at least vacate and remand for application of that stringent exception), not to decide a new merits theory in the first instance on appeal.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to warn that we are a court of review and that a court of appeals’ application of its own forfeiture doctrine is often too factbound to second-guess. But this looks less like a marginal application of a local prudential rule and more like affirmance on a concededly unpreserved theory that was neither pressed nor passed upon below—placing it outside our ordinary “pressed or passed upon” limit. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, even under the Tenth Circuit’s own exception, the premise of “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” is difficult to maintain where the theory turns on a worker-classification/misclassification framework that is typically mixed law-and-fact and was not adversarially tested in the district court. Absent any Freytag-type structural justification, I would enforce preservation principles and reverse (or at least vacate and remand) rather than bless liability-expanding affirmance on a newly minted appellate theory.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that this looks like a factbound, circuit-specific application of a forfeiture exception that we typically would not second-guess. But here the respondent concedes non-preservation, and the Tenth Circuit affirmed liability on that forfeited theory notwithstanding its own stated requirement that the exception apply only when the issue is a pure question of law and the correct result is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt”—a legal threshold that is not plausibly met in a misclassification/statutory-liability setting that depends on record development. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, preservation is the baseline rule, and absent a clear legal basis to depart from it, the court of appeals should not decide (and certainly not affirm liability on) a theory neither pressed nor passed upon below. The proper disposition is to enforce forfeiture (or at minimum vacate and remand for application of the correct stringent exception), rather than effectively expand appellate first-instance decisionmaking.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is institutional: we are ordinarily reluctant to police a court of appeals’ case-specific administration of a prudential forfeiture exception, lest we become a court of first view. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Tenth Circuit did not simply make a marginal call; it invoked an exception that is expressly limited to “pure” legal questions whose correct resolution is “certain,” yet applied it to a misclassification theory whose application depends on merits-adjacent predicates the parties never litigated and the district court never addressed. That disconnect is a legal, administrable error—failure to adhere to the court’s own demanding preservation standard—rather than a discretionary factual judgment, and enforcing forfeiture here respects the trial–appellate division of labor and avoids advisory decisionmaking on an untested liability theory. Consistent with remand-first principles, the proper disposition is to reverse or vacate rather than endorsing affirmance on a forfeited ground.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that we should not turn this case into second-guessing a factbound, circuit-specific forfeiture determination. But what makes this review-worthy is not discretionary line-drawing at the margins; it is that the Tenth Circuit affirmed on a concededly unpreserved liability theory over a timely forfeiture objection, effectively expanding the issues for decision on appeal without a proper basis to excuse the default. As the Chief Justice explains, the Tenth Circuit’s own “pure question of law/certain resolution” exception is demanding, and in a misclassification setting—where application turns on how statutory standards map onto a developed record—an appellate court cannot responsibly deem the answer “beyond reasonable doubt” without doing first-instance work. Given that preservation is nonjurisdictional here, the court of appeals was obliged to enforce forfeiture (or at least apply the stringent exception correctly), rather than decide a new theory in the first instance.

John Roberts.reasoning: The court of appeals should not affirm liability on a theory the respondent failed to preserve below unless it fits a narrow exception for a “pure matter of law” whose proper resolution is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt.” Here, the disputed theory arises in a worker-classification/misclassification setting that is typically fact-intensive and intertwined with merits-adjacent issues, making it unlikely that the correct disposition can be declared “certain” without the record development and adversarial testing that preservation rules are designed to secure. Under my remand-first approach, when the applicability of a newly raised legal theory depends on case-specific factual or legal questions not addressed by the district court, the proper course is to remand rather than decide it in the first instance—absent futility, which has not been shown. The Tenth Circuit’s decision to reach and resolve the forfeited theory therefore exceeded the limited discretion recognized in its own precedents and undermined proper role-allocation between trial and appellate courts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: On this record, the dispositive question is not the underlying statutory merits but whether the Tenth Circuit permissibly applied its own forfeiture doctrine in deciding to reach an admittedly unpreserved argument under its “pure matter of law” and “certain resolution” exception. That sort of circuit-specific preservation determination is highly factbound and ordinarily reflects, at most, a claimed misapplication of a properly stated rule of law—an asserted error that rarely warrants this Court’s intervention, especially absent a square challenge to the preservation ruling itself rather than a merits dispute. And to the extent petitioners would have us decide, in the first instance, whether the forfeited theory satisfied Jarvis/Schaden (or to reach alternative statutory theories not passed on below), we should decline because we are a court of review, not of first view. The better course is to leave the court of appeals’ discretionary enforcement of its own forfeiture framework undisturbed here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Federal courts ordinarily decide only the questions the parties have presented and preserved, and nonjurisdictional objections and theories of liability are generally forfeited when not timely raised. Here, the Tenth Circuit affirmed on a liability-supporting legal theory that respondent did not adequately press below; that is not a jurisdictional prerequisite that the court was obliged to police sua sponte, but a merits theory subject to ordinary preservation rules. Treating the issue as a “pure question of law” does not justify abandoning party-presentation where, as in a misclassification dispute under a federal labor/employment statute, the theory’s application is statute- and fact-sensitive and carries substantial practical consequences that should have been tested in the district court. Under this Court’s cases, the proper course is to enforce forfeiture and require the party to litigate the theory in the normal adversarial sequence, not resurrect it on appeal to expand liability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Tenth Circuit’s affirmance rests on a liability-supporting legal theory that, on this record, was not “raised, preserved, or passed upon” in the proceedings below, and I would not read tea leaves to infer an implicit ruling on an argument the parties did not squarely litigate. Forfeiture is generally nonjurisdictional, but that cuts against the court of appeals treating its “pure question of law” exception as a license to decide a new theory where the district court made no findings and the parties had no fair opportunity to develop the statutory and factual predicates of the misclassification dispute. Nothing in the materials provided shows concrete circumstances excusing the failure to preserve (confusing pleadings, respondent’s substantial presentation in substance, or petitioners’ own forfeiture of a forfeiture objection), so ordinary preservation principles should control. The proper course is to reverse and require adherence to issue-preservation limits rather than expanding liability on appeal on an unpreserved ground.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The baseline rule of appellate preservation is that a party who concedes it failed to raise an argument in the district court has forfeited it, and an appellate court may depart from that rule only under a clearly defined, ordinary standard—not by stretching discretion to reach an unpreserved liability (or defense) theory. Here, respondent admits non-preservation, and under the Tenth Circuit’s own framework the “pure question of law” exception applies only when the correct disposition is certain or beyond reasonable doubt; that is a demanding threshold that cannot be satisfied where the unraised theory would require fresh legal analysis (and potentially factual framing) in the first instance. Consistent with the division of labor between trial and appellate courts, the proper course is not to affirm on a new theory but to enforce ordinary forfeiture principles (or at minimum remand for application of the correct forfeiture standard rather than effectively deciding the case on an untested ground). Nothing in the governing employment statute supplies a carve-out authorizing courts of appeals to entertain forfeited liability theories based on remedial purpose alone.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The threshold question is preservation: respondent concedes it failed to present the liability-supporting theory to the district court, and the court of appeals’ willingness to reach it rests only on a discretionary “pure question of law/certainty” exception. Under the “pressed or passed upon” rule, appellate review is generally improper where the argument was neither pressed by the party nor actually passed upon by the court below; on this record, the theory appears to have been introduced for the first time on appeal rather than decided in the first instance by the district court. Absent a clear structural concern or other exceptional basis to excuse forfeiture, and given the importance of respecting lower courts’ preservation rulings as a constraint on appellate power, I would not endorse affirmance on an unpreserved, newly minted appellate theory. The proper course is to require adherence to ordinary preservation rules rather than expand liability through an argument not litigated below.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The threshold question is preservation: the respondent had an opportunity to present the liability-supporting legal theory in the district court and did not do so, which amounts to forfeiture under ordinary appellate-preservation principles. Once forfeiture is established, the court of appeals should apply the governing discretionary standard for reviewing unpreserved issues, and it may depart from the baseline rule only with a clear legal basis for doing so. The Tenth Circuit’s narrow exception allows consideration of a newly raised legal theory only when it is a pure question of law and the proper resolution is "certain" or "beyond reasonable doubt"; on this misclassification/statutory-liability record, the alternative theory’s correctness is not so certain that it justifies bypassing forfeiture. Affirming liability on an unpreserved theory therefore improperly departs from the default rule that appellate courts do not consider forfeited arguments absent the stringent requirements for discretionary review.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The governing rule is that courts of appeals generally do not consider forfeited theories, and the Tenth Circuit’s own exception applies only when the issue is a “pure matter of law” and its correct resolution is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt.” Here, respondent concededly failed to press the liability theory in the district court, and the misclassification/interstate-commerce questions in this record are at least partly fact-dependent—precisely the kind of setting where an appellate court cannot confidently say the right answer is certain without trenching on factfinding. Under a preservation-focused approach, the court of appeals should not expand liability based on a new theory that was not properly preserved, especially where doing so risks deciding more than is necessary and encourages bypassing orderly presentation below. Because the prerequisites for discretionary review of a forfeited argument are not satisfied on these facts, affirmance on that unpreserved ground was improper.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The preservation rule at issue is not jurisdictional—there is no clear congressional statement making a party’s presentation of a particular legal theory below a jurisdictional prerequisite to appellate review—so it functions as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing doctrine that is ordinarily subject to waiver and forfeiture. Here, petitioners invoked forfeiture, and the Tenth Circuit’s decision to reach and resolve respondent’s newly minted liability theory appears to have enforced an exception without the requisite certainty Jarvis/Avenue Capital demand (i.e., that the issue is a pure question of law and its correct resolution is beyond reasonable doubt). Given that this was a misclassification dispute turning on a federal labor/employment statute and (by its nature) application of legal standards to a developed factual record, the “proper resolution is certain” threshold is not met, and the court of appeals effectively expanded liability on an unpreserved theory. Consistent with this Court’s approach to nonjurisdictional rules, the better course is to hold the theory forfeited absent a properly justified, narrowly applied exception rather than permit an appellate court to supply and decide it over a timely forfeiture objection.
